pl-l2d24c4-d1e108.summary: Distinguishes sensuality, a lower power whose motion tends to the bodily senses and appetite for bodily things, from reason, the higher power, which has two parts: the higher, intent on contemplating or consulting things above, and the lower, attending to temporal arrangements. Whatever in the soul we share with beasts is sensuality; where something first appears not shared with beasts, reason begins.
claims: Reason has higher and lower parts.

pl-l2d24c4-d1e113.summary: Cites De Trinitate XII: let us see where the boundary of outer and inner man is; what we share with animals belongs to the outer man, not just the body but the life by which senses flourish; where we first meet something not shared with beasts, reason begins and the inner man can be recognized.
claims: The outer man includes what we share with beasts.

pl-l2d24c4.summary: Distinguishes sensuality, the lower power of the soul moving toward bodily senses and appetites, from reason, the higher power, which has a higher part, intent on contemplating or consulting things above, and a lower part, attending to temporal affairs. What in the soul we share with beasts belongs to sensuality; where something first appears that we do not share with beasts, reason begins (Augustine, De Trinitate XII: the boundary of outer and inner man).
claims: Sensuality is the lower power, directed to the senses and bodily appetites.
Reason is the higher power, with higher and lower parts.
The higher part of reason looks to things above; the lower to temporal affairs.
What we share with beasts belongs to sensuality; reason begins where we differ.
